conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood, not to judge.  
To get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling, I’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It screens for low mood, anxiety, and—importantly—any thoughts of self-harm in the past seven days. Everything you share stays between us unless safety is at risk, and we’ll move at your pace.

I’ll ask 10 gentle questions; just tell me what feels true for you—no right or wrong answers. Ready to start?

1. In the past week, when you were able to sleep, how did you find your overall rest—did you sleep well, or did things like worry or baby needs keep you up most of the time?

Honestly, even when the baby’s asleep I can’t seem to drift off. My mind keeps circling—what if he spits up and I don’t hear him, what if I’m doing everything wrong… I lie there for ages, and if I do fall asleep I jerk awake once or twice a night with my heart racing. So I guess I’m not really getting much rest at all.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, every now and then something small will make me smile, but it feels like I have to force it. Most of the time I’m just too tired and down to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get a little spark when I think about taking the baby out in the stroller to get a fancy coffee, but it’s nothing like the excitement I used to feel before he was born. Even that coffee thing feels kind of “meh” now—like I’ll probably go, but I’m not really looking forward to it the way I once would have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If he fusses for a long time or won’t nap, I automatically think it’s because I missed some cue or I’m not soothing him right. Even little stuff, like spitting up a lot, I’ll turn around in my head and wonder what I ate that caused it. I know logically it’s not all on me, but the guilty feeling still pops up several times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, but suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to happen—like I’ll picture him stopping breathing or me dropping him. There’s no real trigger; the thoughts just crash in and I can’t shut them off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. It comes out of nowhere—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby monitor or go peek in the crib just to be sure he’s okay. It passes after a bit, but in the moment I feel like something terrible is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, honestly most days feel like that. I’ll be feeding him and notice the dishes piling up, or I’ll hear my phone buzz with messages I haven’t answered, and suddenly it feels like I’m drowning. I usually get through it—no yelling or shutting down completely—but it takes real effort to take the next step without crying.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been my nights lately. I feel this heavy sadness sitting on my chest once the lights go off, and then my brain just keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs.” I’ll lie there for an hour or more before I finally drift off, and even then I wake up a couple of times with my heart pounding. So yeah, the unhappiness is definitely making the sleep even worse.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty often. I’d say most of the day I carry this gray cloud—nothing feels bright or exciting, and sometimes I just want to curl up and cry. It isn’t every single minute, but it’s definitely the main background feeling I’ve had this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Once was when he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and I felt totally useless; the other time was after my mom left from visiting—she closed the door and I just burst into tears, couldn’t stop for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s crossed my mind, just briefly, maybe once or twice. Nothing planned—no real intent—but in those exhausted, overwhelmed moments I’ve thought, “What if I just weren’t here?” Then I feel awful for even thinking it, because I want to be here for my son.

You've shared how most days feel heavy, with little joy, constant self-blame, and an anxious dread that arrives uninvited. Sleep is elusive, tears come easily, and even the small pleasures you can still imagine feel muted. Feeling overwhelmed and, at the lowest moments, briefly wishing you could disappear, you nonetheless hold tight to your love for your baby and your wish to be there for him.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports having to force laughter, rarely finding things funny, and feeling too down to laugh, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably diminished enjoyment and anticipation, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "several times a day" for normal infant behaviors, which aligns with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive anxious thoughts occurring daily without clear triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports unexpected panic episodes "a few times this week," matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm but still manages to function without total collapse, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating sleep due to unhappiness and racing thoughts, plus mid-sleep waking with anxiety—semantic match to "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"—patient reports sadness "most of the day" as main feeling this week.</sym>, <sym>Twice in a week, with one prolonged episode, maps to "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map closely to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day (<sym>gray cloud</sym>), markedly diminished interest (<sym>fancy coffee feels meh</sym>), guilt (<sym>what I ate that caused it</sym>), concentration difficulty (<sym>mind keeps circling</sym>), sleep disturbance (<sym>heavy sadness on chest</sym>), and fatigue. Combined score 23 (≥14) plus Item 10 ≥1 signals high risk requiring urgent assessment. <quote>What if I just weren't here?</quote> indicates passive suicidal ideation without intent, still mandating safety plan. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> for full evaluation
2. Request immediate perinatal mental-health referral (therapy and medication options)
3. Complete safety plan now: remove dangerous items, list 24/7 supports and hotlines (e.g., 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline)
4. Encourage practical daily support-partner/friend to handle night bottle, meals, chores
5. Practice brief <med>breathing exercises</med> and 5-minute outdoor walks to reduce <sym>physiological arousal</sym>
6. Schedule pediatric check within days so baby's wellbeing and your feeding mood can be reviewed together
7. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Note – Postpartum Period (Not Diagnostic)

Presenting symptoms/concerns endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious worries and occasional panic symptoms  
- Sleep disruption directly linked to mood distress  
- Feeling “overwhelmed” or “drowning” most days  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan or intent)

Pattern:
Consistent with possible depressive and anxiety spectrum presentation in postpartum context; functional impact evident (sleep, coping, emotional regulation).

Risk flags:
- Passive SI (safety factor)  
- Significant emotional distress, impaired functioning, limited reported support at present

Screening significance: High likelihood for postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; warrants immediate formal assessment, safety planning, and discussion of support/treatment options.
